title: How to fix the slow checkout line
description:
With 4 separate checkout lines, yours is the fastest only one time in four, and one slow shopper freezes a whole lane. One snake line feeding whichever till frees up first fixes it. In a simulation with 4 tills, a shopper every 37.5 seconds, 2 minutes per checkout and one shopper in 10 slow, the average wait drops by a quarter (about 2.9 to 2.2 minutes), the unluckiest 1 in 100 waits 17 minutes instead of 26, and nobody gets overtaken (with separate lines, nearly 1 in 3 shoppers do). Queueing theory started with Agner Erlang in 1909, sizing Copenhagen's telephone network.

Numbers checked in code (400,000-shopper simulations over 5 seeds). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agner_Krarup_Erlang https://www.qminder.com/blog/queue-management/single-line-vs-multiple-line-queues/

beats.say: You run a supermarket, and your customers are furious: they always pick the slow line. Here's how you fix it.
First, they're right. With 4 lines, yours is the fastest only one time in four. Three times in four, another line wins.
And one slow shopper with a price check freezes a whole line, while the next till runs empty.
So tear down the lanes. Build one snake line, and send whoever is at the front to the first free till.
Test it. 4 tills, a shopper every 37.5 seconds, 2 minutes each at the till, and one in 10 is slow.
The average wait drops by a quarter. And the unluckiest shopper in 100 waited 26 minutes. Now, 17.
With separate lines, nearly one in three shoppers get overtaken by someone who came in later. With one line, nobody.
Uh-oh. The snake looks huge, and people turn around at the door.
So show it moving. With 4 tills, it steps forward every 30 seconds. And a screen calls the next free till.
And there you have it: shorter waits, no unlucky lanes, and nobody cutting ahead.
This is queueing theory. Agner Erlang started it in 1909, sizing Copenhagen's phone network. It's why banks and airports use one line.
